extracted.intended_audience: researchers and developers of formal proof assistants, Mizar users, and mathematical-knowledge-management researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for building, organizing, maintaining, and using the Mizar Mathematical Library (MML) as a centrally-managed repository of formalized mathematics, including choices of axiomatization, data storage, import/export mechanisms, revision policies, and automation features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulate and enable re-use of previously formalized knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The library should accumulate all previously available formalized knowledge so that new works can effectively re-use previously collected notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MML was created to avoid duplication and to provide organized libraries accumulating prior formalizations; this approach supports large-scale formalizations and enables efficient reuse across articles and projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrally-managed knowledge base maintained with language and verifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the library as a centrally-managed knowledge base together with the formalization language and the verification system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The turning point for Mizar was building the MML as a centrally-managed knowledge base maintained with the language and the checker, enabling consistent interfaces, revisions, and shared axiomatizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article as basic import/export unit and use of abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic library import/export unit is an article; exportable items are selected and extracted to form an 'abstract' that contains bare statements stripped of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors initially decide which definitions and statements to export; during peer review the exportable items are finalized and stored in XML-based internal database formats. Abstracts are the public interface used for the database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review coordinated by the Library Committee for selecting exported items
rubrics_metrics.description: A Library Committee coordinates peer review to select which items in an article are exportable to the MML abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee process ensures consistent and curated selection of exportable definitions, theorems, schemes and registrations for the shared library interface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad-hoc axiomatization and contradictory environment declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing arbitrary user-declared environments that can introduce contradictory items or ad-hoc axiomatics for each article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier Mizar versions put environment declaration responsibility on users, lengthening preparation time and risking contradictions; the MML design aims to prevent ad-hoc axioms and minimize contradictions by centralizing exported items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement and prefer minimal axiomatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a minimal axiomatization for articles: import only necessary items to establish a minimal set of axioms for a given article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation and consequent use of minimal axiomatization lets library development focus on language extensions and automation rather than hard-coded procedures; it reduces risk of contradictions and repeated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a consistent foundational axiomatization (Tarski–Grothendieck chosen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and standardize the library on a coherent foundation (Mizar chose Tarski–Grothendieck set theory), while allowing the system to remain, in principle, independent of a particular set theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MML experimented with several foundations before selecting TG; the library structure (e.g., TARSKI_0, TARSKI_A, TARSKI) and axiomatic files reflect the need to balance usability and theoretical foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store exported semantic information in an XML-based database using constructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Exported items (definitions, theorems, schemes, registrations) are stored in the database in dedicated XML-based internal data formats represented using constructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The database contains formulas represented with different kinds of constructors (attribute, functor, mode, predicate, selector, structure); this enables semantic processing, queries and downstream tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate vocabularies (symbols/notations) from articles to allow multiple notations and overloading
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep symbol vocabularies separate from the articles that introduce them to facilitate using symbols for multiple notations and to support overloading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation permits the same format to be used for arguments with different types and enables multiple notations per symbol; it also makes ordering of vocabularies important for disambiguation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit import directives to control amount of imported information
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply a set of designated Mizar directives (vocabularies, constructors, registrations, requirements, expansions, equalities) to control import and disambiguation of formal texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directives allow fine-grained control over overloaded notations and built-in automation; because of overloading the order of used notations is important and different directives influence how the checker applies automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use librarian/extractor/accommodator tools for efficient import/export
rubrics_metrics.description: Use utilities (historically librarian, later extractor and accommodator) to include notions from previously processed files into new articles efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The librarian approach of copying generated files proved inefficient for large formalizations; extractor/accommodator extract semantic information into a database and include needed information into new formalizations, avoiding full environment copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store notation format and type information with each definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For each definition the database stores the definiens, the notation (format), and type information about arguments and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format contains the symbol string, arity and positions of visible arguments; this supports precise rendering, disambiguation, and automated processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide registrations and properties to enable proof-checker automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare properties (e.g., reflexivity, commutativity) and registrations (conditional, existential, functorial, term identification, term reduction) to enable and control automation in the proof checker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrations are heavily used in Mizar (table of registration counts); 'requirements' let users decide whether certain facts (like arithmetic) should be considered automatically obvious to the checker and can be switched off for educational/experimental contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow switching off automation for education and experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide mechanisms (e.g., requirements) to switch off built-in automation so users can teach proof writing or experiment with different axiomatic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automation improves usability but must be controllable; corresponding ordinary Mizar articles justify automatically-obvious facts to allow toggling automation safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and monitor library metrics (constructors, symbols, theorems/definitions ratio, registrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect quantitative metrics (number of constructors, notations, definitions, theorems, registrations) to understand library composition and reuse patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tables showing counts of constructors, symbols, registrations and a theorem/definition ratio (~4.95 or 6.15 if counting registrations) inform library development and tooling priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fine-grained dependency analysis and modularize axiomatic files
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze fine-grained dependencies to reorganize axiomatic files (e.g., splitting TARSKI into TARSKI_0, TARSKI_A, TARSKI) so that raw axioms and user-friendly consequences are cleanly separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such modularization aids reasoning about dependencies, simplifies user-facing formulations, and supports better import granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt revision mechanisms to maintain uniformity and integrity: authored, automatic, pretty-printing, reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use several revision types—authored (small edits by submitters), automatic (tool-driven simplifications), pretty-printing (non-exported cosmetic changes), and reorganization (changing article processing order)—to maintain and evolve the library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisions evolved from a liberal acceptance policy to continuous, intensive revisions. Automatic revisions may rely on improved verifier or new language features; reorganizations use mml.lar to control processing order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group and order articles (mml.lar) to isolate frequently revised parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage the order of article processing (mml.lar) and group articles into parts (concrete, abstract, SCM) to isolate parts requiring frequent revisions and reduce cascading updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2001 reorganization grouped non-structure articles (concrete) before structure-dependent ones (abstract) and isolated the SCM part at the end to allow frequent changes without forcing broad updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage centralized maintenance to enable large-scale collaboration and diverse contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A centrally maintained library enables researchers from many groups to collaborate, contributing diverse parts of the library corresponding to areas of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MML authorship statistics show contributions from many countries and groups; central maintenance allowed international projects (e.g., Compendium of Continuous Lattices) and large formalization efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate and reduce duplication while accommodating heterogeneous formalisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Design mechanisms to manage heterogeneous theories and different representations (e.g., lattices as algebraic structures vs ordered sets) and to detect/remove duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects like CCL required handling multiple representations and motivated tools for managing heterogeneous theories and revisions to reduce duplication and reconcile related objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent term reductions and identifications syntactically as registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Term reductions and identifications are represented syntactically in the database as registrations so they participate in automation and retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cataloguing these as registrations integrates them into the proof checker’s automation mechanisms and into library metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make exported interface machine-processable for retrieval and automated tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Store exported abstracts and semantic data in machine-readable formats (XML/constructors) to enable semantic processing, queries (MML Query), translation, and automated theorem proving tools (MPTP, MizAR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The XML-ized MML and constructor-based representations facilitate information retrieval, proof presentation, cross-verification with ATPs, and statistics-driven tooling (e.g., premise selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control symbol overloading by ordering and import directives
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of heavy overloading, the order of used notations and import directives matters for disambiguation and correct processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users must carefully manage vocabularies and the order of imported notations to ensure deterministic parsing and to avoid ambiguity introduced by multiple notations for the same symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide measures of information transfer between articles (theorem dependence) for library analytics
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify information transfer by analyzing references (use of 'by') and compute measures (Shannon-based) to identify ancestors, children, and long dependence chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amount of information transferred by a theorem into another article is calculated (I = a - log2(n/N)) helping identify central articles (e.g., FINSEQ_1 with many children) and long dependency chains used in library analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage documenting and justifying automation and definitional expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Automation and definitional expansions should be accompanied by ordinary Mizar articles that justify the automated facts to allow cross-verification and safe toggling of automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice ensures that automatically-obvious facts have formal justification in the library, supporting reproducibility, educational uses, and experiments with alternative axiomatizations.
